name: Apple - Apple scab
description: Apple foliage affected by Apple scab. Fungal disease caused primarily by Alternaria species, producing characteristic concentric target-board lesions on foliage.
symptoms: Brown to black spots with concentric rings surrounded by yellow chlorotic halos, beginning on lower/older leaves and advancing upward.
causes: Alternaria solani spores surviving in infected plant debris; favored by alternating wet and dry conditions with high humidity.
organic_treatment: Apply cold-pressed neem oil (0.5%) or bio-fungicide containing Bacillus subtilis / Trichoderma harzianum weekly.
chemical_treatment: Foliar application of Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or Copper hydroxide sprays at 7–10 day intervals.
prevention: Practice 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops. Apply organic mulch around base to stop soil splash.

name: Apple - Black rot
description: Apple foliage affected by Black rot. Destructive fungal disease affecting apples and grapes causing necrotic leaf lesions and fruit mummification.
symptoms: Circular reddish-brown spots that develop tiny black specks (pycnidia) in the center; infected leaves turn yellow and drop.
causes: Botryosphaeria obtusa / Guignardia bidwellii overwintering in mummified fruit, dead wood, and fallen cankers.
organic_treatment: Thorough dormant-season sanitation; apply liquid copper or sulfur sprays at bud break.
chemical_treatment: Captan, Mancozeb, or Myclobutanil fungicides applied from early bud stage through post-bloom.
prevention: Prune out dead canes and cankers during winter; destroy all mummified fruits left on the vine/tree.

name: Apple - Cedar apple rust
description: Apple foliage affected by Cedar apple rust. Fungal disease producing powdery rust-colored pustules on leaf undersides.
symptoms: Small, raised orange, yellow, or cinnamon-brown pustules that break through leaf epidermis, releasing powdery spores.
causes: Puccinia species spores carried by wind over long distances; favored by moderate temperatures and dew.
organic_treatment: Foliar application of sulfur dust or neem oil; bio-control with Ampelomyces quisqualis.
chemical_treatment: Triazole fungicides (Propiconazole, Tebuconazole) or Strobilurins (Azoxystrobin).
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids. Remove alternate host weeds (like juniper for cedar apple rust) nearby.

name: Apple - healthy

symptoms: Intact leaf structure, consistent green pigmentation, absence of lesions, spots, curling, or necrosis.
causes: Optimal watering, balanced N-P-K nutrient availability, and good air circulation.

chemical_treatment: No chemical fungicide or pesticide required. Maintain balanced micronutrient foliar sprays if needed.
prevention: Ensure proper spacing between crops to promote air circulation and avoid overhead leaf wetting.

symptoms: White to light gray powdery patches on the upper and lower leaf surfaces, leading to leaf yellowing, curling, and premature leaf drop.

chemical_treatment: Sulfur-based dusts or systemic fungicides like Myclobutanil or Azoxystrobin applied every 10–14 days.
prevention: Select resistant cultivars, prune dense foliage to maximize sunlight penetration and airflow.

name: Peach - Bacterial spot
description: Peach foliage affected by Bacterial spot. Bacterial infection caused by Xanthomonas species attacking leaves, stems, and fruit under warm, rainy weather.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked circular lesions that turn dark brown or black with a distinct yellow halo, giving leaves a ragged appearance.

prevention: Disinfect pruning tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol between plants. Avoid working in fields when foliage is wet.

name: Potato - Late blight
description: Potato foliage affected by Late blight. Devastating oomycete pathogen caused by Phytophthora infestans that rapidly spreads and can destroy entire fields within days under cool, humid conditions.
symptoms: Large irregular water-soaked pale-green to dark-brown lesions with fuzzy white sporulation on leaf undersides in humid mornings.
causes: Phytophthora infestans favored by prolonged leaf moisture (>10 hours) and temperatures between 15°C and 22°C.
organic_treatment: Apply fixed copper sprays (Bordeaux mixture) preventively. Remove and deeply bury or burn severely infected leaves immediately.
chemical_treatment: Systemic fungicides: Metalaxyl + Mancozeb, Cymoxanil, or Dimethomorph applied preventively or upon first symptom.
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds/tubers. Avoid overhead irrigation and ensure rapid foliage drying through wide row spacing.

name: Tomato - Leaf Mold
description: Tomato foliage affected by Leaf Mold. Foliar fungal pathogen caused by Passalora fulva common in high-humidity greenhouse environments.
symptoms: Pale green to yellowish spots on upper leaf surface, with olive-green to grayish velvety mold on the underside.
causes: Relative humidity above 85% with temperatures around 21°C–24°C.
organic_treatment: Copper fungicides and bio-fungicides; improve greenhouse ventilation and exhaust fan circulation.
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil, Copper sulfate, or Difenoconazole.
prevention: Maintain greenhouse relative humidity below 80% with heated airflow and drip irrigation.

name: Tomato - Septoria leaf spot
description: Tomato foliage affected by Septoria leaf spot. Fungal disease caused by Septoria lycopersici causing numerous small circular leaf spots with dark borders.
symptoms: Numerous small (1.5-3mm) circular spots with gray or tan centers and dark brown margins with black pycnidia.
causes: Septoria lycopersici surviving on solanaceous weeds and crop residue, splashed by raindrops.
organic_treatment: Copper soap fungicides applied at 7-day intervals; bottom pruning lower 12 inches of foliage.
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb sprays immediately after first bottom lesions appear.
prevention: Crop rotation, drip irrigation, and heavy straw mulching to prevent soil splashing onto leaves.

name: Tomato - Spider mites Two-spotted spider mite
description: Tomato foliage affected by Spider mites Two-spotted spider mite. Arachnid pests (Tetranychus urticae) that suck plant sap and cause chlorotic stippling.
symptoms: Fine white/yellow stippling on upper leaf surface, bronze discoloration, and fine silken webbing on leaf undersides.
causes: Hot, dry, dusty environmental conditions accelerating the mite reproduction cycle to just 5 days.
organic_treatment: Insecticidal soap or horticultural mineral oil sprays; release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis).
chemical_treatment: Miticide sprays containing Abamectin, Bifenazate, or Spiromesifen; avoid broad-spectrum pyrethroids that kill natural predators.
prevention: Keep foliage and access pathways misted or watered to reduce dust; inspect undersides of leaves weekly.

name: Tomato - Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
description: Tomato foliage affected by Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus. Systemic viral infections causing severe stunted growth, chlorosis, and leaf deformation.
symptoms: Mottled yellow-green mosaic patterns, upward leaf curling, crinkling, stunted internodes, and brittle foliage.
causes: Transmitted by insect vectors like whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci), aphids, thrips, or mechanical contact.
organic_treatment: Vector control with reflective silver mulches, yellow sticky traps, and neem-based insecticidal sprays.
chemical_treatment: Control insect vectors with Imidacloprid, Acetamiprid, or Flonicamid. Note: Viral infections cannot be cured with fungicides.
prevention: Rogue out and destroy infected plants immediately; install 50-mesh insect screens in greenhouses.
